## Parallel directions {#fv4-parallel .fv-lesson .relation-lesson }

```{=html}
<p>Two lines have parallel directions when their non-zero direction vectors satisfy</p><div class="fv-equation"><span data-math="\underset{\sim}{d_2}=k\underset{\sim}{d_1},\qquad k\ne0"></span></div><div class="relation-split"><div><h3>In two dimensions</h3><div class="fv-equation"><span data-math="\color{#315985}{\begin{bmatrix}-6\\3\end{bmatrix}}=\color{#ad6e32}{-3}\color{#217864}{\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\end{bmatrix}}"></span></div></div><div><h3>In three dimensions</h3><div class="fv-equation"><span data-math="\color{#315985}{\begin{bmatrix}-4\\2\\-6\end{bmatrix}}=\color{#ad6e32}{-2}\color{#217864}{\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{bmatrix}}"></span></div></div></div><p class="relation-key">One scalar multiplies <strong>every</strong> component.</p><p>A negative scalar reverses the direction; the lines still have parallel directions.</p>
```

<div class="booklet-cue">Booklet §3.3 · pp. 51–52</div>

::: {.notes}
The two numerical comparisons are additional illustrations, not booklet examples. Non-zero direction vectors are required. Explain that proportional directions alone do not distinguish distinct parallel lines from coincident lines; the next slide checks a fixed point. Do not use component-by-component division when a direction component is zero: test multiplication by the same scalar instead. In both 2D and 3D the criterion is the same.
:::
